cards.back: Ask the model to reason step by step before answering, in one call. Best when all the facts are already in the prompt; it can't fetch facts it doesn't know.
A loop of thought, tool call and observation, repeated until the agent can answer. Fits tasks that need tools or fresh data where each step depends on the last. Cap the steps.
Propose several next thoughts, score partial solutions, keep the promising branches and backtrack. Worth its many calls only when early choices decide everything and progress can be scored.
A strong planner writes all the steps once; a cheaper executor runs them. Fewer expensive calls, parallel steps and a plan a person can approve, but rigid without re-planning.
After a check fails, the agent writes what went wrong and retries with that note. Prefer a real check (tests, schema) over pure self-critique, and cap retries at 2 or 3.
Each outcome's cost or gain weighted by its probability, summed. Under uncertainty, pick the action with the best expected value.
40% closure, reroute $12k, closure $50k. Keeping the route costs 0.4 × $50k = $20k on average, more than $12k, so reroute. Break-even is 12 ÷ 50 = 24%.
With a perfect forecast you'd reroute only when the port closes: 0.4 × $12k = $4.8k. Best without it is $12k, so perfect information is worth at most $7.2k.
Conclusions that must be true from rules and known facts. It stalls when a needed fact is only likely or missing, as with incomplete sensor data.

cards.front: Rule-based threshold matching vs expected value
cards.back: A fixed cutoff such as 'act above 50%' looks at the probability but not the costs. The right cutoff is cost ÷ loss, so it moves whenever the costs change.
A rule of thumb scores options and drops weak ones fast (best-first, beam, A*). It suits large search spaces, not a single bet on an uncertain outcome.

quiz.q: A logistics agent must decide whether to reroute around a port with a 40% chance of storm closure. Sensor data is incomplete, rerouting costs $12k and a closure would cost $50k. Which reasoning approach fits best?
quiz.why: An uncertain outcome with known costs calls for weighing probability × cost: $20k expected against $12k certain, so reroute.

quiz.q: In the storm example, a rule says 'reroute if closure is more likely than not'. What does it do at 40%, and is that right?
choices: Keeps the route, which is wrong: rerouting is cheaper on average
Keeps the route, which is right because 40% is under 50%
Asks a person, because 40% is uncertain
quiz.why: The 50% cutoff ignores the costs; the break-even is 24%, so at 40% rerouting saves $8k on average.

quiz.q: Rerouting costs $12k and a closure costs $50k. Above what closure probability should the agent reroute?
quiz.why: Reroute when p × $50k > $12k, so when p > 12 ÷ 50 = 24%.

quiz.q: An agent needs live data and can't predict which lookup comes next. Which pattern fits?
quiz.why: ReAct interleaves thinking with tool calls, so each observation decides the next step.

quiz.q: Month-end close across 200 invoices: steps are known, cost matters and a manager must approve the work first. Which pattern fits?
quiz.why: Known steps, parallel cheap execution and a visible plan to approve; re-planning recovers from failed steps.

quiz.q: Why should an agent compute expected value in a tool rather than in the model's reasoning?
choices: Code is exact and testable; mental arithmetic in a model is neither
Tools are cheaper than tokens in every case
quiz.why: Let tools supply the probability and costs, and do the arithmetic in code you can test and log.

quiz.q: Code must pass unit tests and first attempts often fail. What do you add?
choices: A reflection loop that uses the test results, with a retry cap
Tree of thoughts over every line
quiz.why: Tests give a real check to reflect on; cap retries at 2 or 3.
